(1) the performance of a client-server system is highly sensitive to the amount of data that is cached at the clients, and (2) the performance of the system can be improved significantly by caching data at the clients.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no one best cache consistency algorithm, but that the best choice of cache consistency algorithm depends on the relative cost of the various system resources and the nature of the application workload.
the performance tradeoff between lockbased and optimistic consistency is workload dependent.
there are no clear winners in the race for the best cache consistency algorithm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the best cache consistency algorithm is one that minimizes the number of data items that must be fetched from the server to maintain consistency, and that the number of items that must be retrieved is directly related to the degree of concurrency that is allowed in the client workloads.
, in the client-server environment, the use of client caches can significantly improve performance, but only when the client cache is large enough to hold the most frequently accessed data.
client-server caching can be an effective performance enhancement, but that the performance of the cache is sensitive to the workload and the cache configuration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to achieve good performance in a client-server environment, the cache consistency mechanism must be tailored to match the workload and the system configuration.
the choice of a cache consistency algorithm should be based on the expected workload, the amount of client memory, and the cost of communication with the server.
the performance tradeoffs in clientserver cache consistency can be quite different from those in traditional replicated database systems.
